blocks.text: K. stared at the inspector. Was he being given schoolroom lessons here by a man perhaps younger than himself? Was he being punished for his frankness with a reprimand? And was he to learn nothing of the reason for his arrest or of those who had ordered it?

He grew somewhat agitated, walked up and down, which no one prevented him from doing, pushed back his cuffs, felt his chest, smoothed his hair, passed the three gentlemen, said, “It is all quite senseless,” whereupon they turned towards him and looked at him obligingly but gravely, and finally came to a halt once more before the inspector’s table. “The public prosecutor Hasterer is a good friend of mine,” he said, “may I telephone him?” “Certainly,” said the inspector, “but I do not know what purpose that would serve, unless you have some private matter to discuss with him.” “What purpose?” cried K., more dismayed than annoyed. “Who are you, then? You ask for a purpose and carry on in the most senseless manner imaginable. Is it not enough to move a stone? These gentlemen first fell upon me, and now they sit or stand about here and make me perform feats of dressage before you. What purpose would it serve to telephone a public prosecutor when I am supposedly under arrest? Very well, I shall not telephone.” “But do,” said the inspector, stretching out his hand towards the hall, where the telephone was, “please do telephone.” “No, I no longer wish to,” said K., and went to the window. Across the way the party was still at the window and seemed only now, because K. had come to the window, to be somewhat disturbed in its tranquil watching. The old people were about to rise, but the man behind them reassured them. “There are more spectators over there,” K. called very loudly to the inspector, pointing outside with his forefinger. “Away from there,” he then called across. The three did at once retreat a few steps, the two old people even behind the man, who screened them with his broad body and, to judge by the movements of his mouth, said something unintelligible at that distance. They did not disappear altogether, however, but seemed to be waiting for the moment when they could approach the window again unnoticed. “Intrusive, inconsiderate people!” said K. as he turned back into the room. The inspector possibly agreed with him, as K. thought he could discern from a sidelong glance. But it was equally possible that he had not listened at all, for he had pressed one hand firmly upon the table and seemed to be comparing the lengths of his fingers. The two warders were sitting on a trunk covered with an ornamental cloth and rubbing their knees. The three young men had put their hands on their hips and were looking aimlessly about. It was as quiet as in some forgotten office. “Well, gentlemen,” cried K., for a moment it seemed to him as though he bore them all upon his shoulders, “to judge by your appearance, my affair would seem to be concluded. I am of the opinion that it would be best to think no further about whether your proceedings are justified or unjustified, and to bring the matter to an amicable conclusion by shaking hands. If you share my opinion, then pray”—and he stepped up to the inspector’s table and held out his hand. The inspector raised his eyes, gnawed at his lips and looked at K.’s outstretched hand; K. still believed that the inspector would take it. But instead he rose, took a stiff round hat that lay on Fräulein Bürstner’s bed and put it on carefully with both hands, as one does when trying on a new hat. “How simple everything seems to you!” he said to K. as he did so, “we ought to bring the matter to an amicable conclusion, you thought? No, no, that really will not do. By which, on the other hand, I certainly do not mean to say that you should despair. No, why should you? You are merely under arrest, nothing more. That was what I had to tell you, I have done so, and I have also seen how you have taken it. That is enough for today, and we may take our leave, though only for the present. You will presumably wish to go to the bank now?” “To the bank?” asked K., “I thought I was under arrest.” K. asked with a certain defiance, for although his offered handshake had not been accepted, he felt increasingly independent of all these people, particularly since the inspector had risen. He was playing with them. He intended, should they leave, to run after them as far as the front door and offer himself up for arrest. That was also why he repeated: “How can I go to the bank when I am under arrest?” “Ah, I see,” said the inspector, who was already at the door, “you have misunderstood me. You are under arrest, certainly, but that is not to prevent you from attending to your profession. Nor are you to be hindered in your ordinary way of life.” “Then being under arrest is not so very bad,” said K., going close up to the inspector. “I never meant otherwise,” said the latter. “But in that case even the announcement of the arrest would hardly seem to have been necessary,” said K., drawing still closer. The others too had drawn near. They were all now gathered in a narrow space by the door. “It was my duty,” said the inspector. “A foolish duty,” said K. unyieldingly. “Perhaps,” replied the inspector, “but let us not waste our time with such talk. I had assumed that you wished to go to the bank. Since you attend to every word, I shall add: I am not compelling you to go to the bank, I had merely assumed that you wished to. And to make that easier for you, and to make your arrival at the bank as inconspicuous as possible, I have kept these three gentlemen, your colleagues, here at your disposal.” “What?” cried K., staring at the three in astonishment. These young men, so lacking in distinction and so anaemic, whom he still remembered only as a group beside the photographs, were indeed clerks from his bank, not colleagues, that was saying too much and already revealed a gap in the inspector’s omniscience, but subordinate clerks from the bank they certainly were. How could K. have overlooked this? How absorbed he must have been in the inspector and the warders, not to recognise these three. The stiff Rabensteiner, swinging his hands, fair-haired Kullich with his deep-set eyes, and Kaminer with his unbearable smile, caused by a chronic muscular strain, “Good morning!” said K. after a little while, shaking hands with the gentlemen, who bowed correctly. “I did not recognise you at all. Well, we shall go to work now, shall we not?” The gentlemen nodded eagerly, laughing, as though they had been waiting for this all along, only when K. missed his hat, which had been left in his room, they all ran one after the other to fetch it, which did after all suggest a certain embarrassment. K. stood still and watched them through the two open doors; the last was naturally the indifferent Rabensteiner, who had merely broken into an elegant trot. Kaminer handed him the hat, and K. had to remind himself expressly, as indeed was often necessary at the bank, that Kaminer’s smile was not intentional, indeed that he could not smile intentionally at all. In the hall Frau Grubach, who did not look particularly conscious of guilt, then opened the flat door for the whole party, and K. looked down, as he so often did, at her apron-string, which cut so needlessly deep into her mighty body. Downstairs K., watch in hand, decided to take a motor-car, so as not needlessly to add to his lateness, which already amounted to half an hour. Kaminer ran to the corner to fetch the car, the other two were plainly trying to divert K., when suddenly Kullich pointed to the doorway of the house opposite, where the tall man with the fair pointed beard was just appearing and, at the first moment, somewhat embarrassed at now showing himself at his full height, stepped back to the wall and leaned against it. The old people were probably still on the stairs. K. was annoyed with Kullich for drawing attention to the man, whom he himself had seen earlier, indeed whom he had even been expecting. “Do not look over there,” he burst out, without noticing how extraordinary such a manner of speaking was towards independent men. But no explanation was needed either, for just then the motor-car arrived, they seated themselves and drove off. Then K. remembered that he had not noticed the departure of the inspector and the warders at all; the inspector had concealed the three clerks from him, and now in turn the clerks had concealed the inspector. This showed little presence of mind, and K. resolved to observe himself more closely in this respect. Yet he still turned involuntarily and leaned forward over the rear of the motor-car, in the hope of perhaps catching another glimpse of the inspector and the warders. But at once he turned back again and settled comfortably into the corner of the car without having so much as attempted to look for anyone. Although it did not appear so, he would have needed encouragement just then, but now the gentlemen seemed weary, Rabensteiner was looking out of the car to the right, Kullich to the left, and only Kaminer was available with his grin, about which humanity unfortunately forbade one to make a joke.
